article.headline: Sam Altman's Thirty-Year Manifesto on a Life Well Lived
article.lede: In 2015, shortly after turning 30 and roughly eight months before co-founding OpenAI, Sam Altman published a 36-point essay on his blog titled 'The days are long but the decades are short.' The piece began as a candid answer to a friend's question about what he'd learned in a decade. It has circulated ever since.
article.body:
The essay predates Altman's current fame as chief executive of OpenAI and was written while he served as president of the startup accelerator *Y Combinator*. That context shapes the advice: it is conspicuously Silicon Valley in places — surround yourself with ambitious people, take career risks early, aim to be the best in the world at your profession — yet it also reaches for something less mercenary. Several points concern relationships, forgiveness, and gratitude in language that would fit comfortably in a letter to a younger sibling.

The most practically interesting maxim may be point 13: 'Keep your **personal burn rate** low. This alone will give you a lot of opportunities in life.' *Burn rate* is a startup-finance term for the monthly rate at which a company spends cash before reaching profitability. Altman applies it to personal finances: the less you need to sustain your life, the more freedom you have to walk away from the wrong job, take the risky bet, or simply wait.

Some of the maxims sit in quiet tension with Altman's professional circumstances. Point 6 urges readers to 'read more long content and less tweets' — advice now circulated almost exclusively via tweet, and from a CEO whose company's products are widely credited with shortening attention spans. Point 28, 'Don't chase status. Status without substance doesn't work for long,' is harder to square with an executive who has become one of the most visible figures in a notoriously status-conscious industry. Whether the ironies undercut the advice or simply illustrate its difficulty is left to the reader.

The essay's durability owes something to its form — numbered, short, conversational — but also to a genuine tension it names without resolving. The title's claim, that days feel interminable while decades vanish, is a common parental lament repurposed as a productivity warning. Altman's version is a reminder that the gap between intention and action grows imperceptibly until suddenly it doesn't.

concepts.definition: Borrowed from startup finance, where burn rate measures how fast a company spends cash before becoming profitable. Applied to personal life, it means monthly living expenses. Keeping it low preserves optionality — the freedom to change direction without financial pressure forcing the decision.

The mental overhead required to hold information in working memory and manage competing demands. In productivity writing, it refers to the drag created by notifications, unresolved tasks, and low-stakes decisions that consume attention without producing meaningful output. Reducing it means clearing space for work that actually matters.

A Silicon Valley startup accelerator founded in 2005 that funds early-stage companies in exchange for a small equity stake and provides intensive mentorship. Its alumni include Airbnb, Dropbox, and Stripe. Altman served as its president from 2014 to 2019 before leaving to lead OpenAI full-time.
